#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Exact finite demonstrations inspired by the topology of surreal numbers.

The full surreal line is not a finite numerical object.  These examples use
Fractions to demonstrate three proof patterns exactly:
(1) diagonalizing below a finite positive family,
(2) defeating a finite proposal of neighborhoods of zero, and
(3) escaping every finite selection from an unbounded lower-ray cover.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from dataclasses import dataclass
from fractions import Fraction
from typing import Iterable, Sequence


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class DiagonalCertificate:
    """A positive number certified to lie below every listed positive value."""

    inputs: tuple[Fraction, ...]
    bound: Fraction

    def verify(self) -> bool:
        return self.bound > 0 and all(self.bound < value for value in self.inputs)


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class NeighborhoodCertificate:
    """Witnesses that no listed symmetric neighborhood fits in (-infinity, d)."""

    radii: tuple[Fraction, ...]
    selected_points: tuple[Fraction, ...]
    cutoff: Fraction

    def verify(self) -> bool:
        return (
            len(self.radii) == len(self.selected_points)
            and self.cutoff > 0
            and all(radius > 0 for radius in self.radii)
            and all(
                0 < point < radius and point > self.cutoff
                for radius, point in zip(self.radii, self.selected_points)
            )
        )


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class CoverEscapeCertificate:
    """A point lying beyond every endpoint of finitely many lower rays."""

    endpoints: tuple[Fraction, ...]
    escape_point: Fraction

    def verify(self) -> bool:
        return bool(self.endpoints) and all(
            self.escape_point >= endpoint for endpoint in self.endpoints
        )


def as_positive_tuple(values: Iterable[Fraction]) -> tuple[Fraction, ...]:
    """Validate and freeze a nonempty family of positive rational values."""

    frozen = tuple(values)
    if not frozen:
        raise ValueError("at least one value is required")
    if any(value <= 0 for value in frozen):
        raise ValueError("all values must be strictly positive")
    return frozen


def finite_diagonal_bound(values: Iterable[Fraction]) -> DiagonalCertificate:
    """Return half the minimum of a finite positive rational family.

    Time complexity is O(n); auxiliary space is O(n) because the iterable is
    frozen for certificate reporting (the minimum itself needs only O(1)).
    """

    frozen = as_positive_tuple(values)
    certificate = DiagonalCertificate(frozen, min(frozen) / 2)
    assert certificate.verify()
    return certificate


def stress_test_neighborhoods(
    radii: Iterable[Fraction],
) -> NeighborhoodCertificate:
    """Defeat finitely many symmetric neighborhoods (-r_i, r_i).

    Select u_i = r_i/2 in each neighborhood, then choose a positive cutoff d
    below every u_i.  Since u_i > d, no neighborhood is contained in the lower
    ray (-infinity, d).  The computation takes O(n) time.
    """

    frozen = as_positive_tuple(radii)
    selected = tuple(radius / 2 for radius in frozen)
    cutoff = min(selected) / 2
    certificate = NeighborhoodCertificate(frozen, selected, cutoff)
    assert certificate.verify()
    return certificate


def escape_finite_lower_rays(
    endpoints: Sequence[Fraction],
) -> CoverEscapeCertificate:
    """Find a point omitted by every lower ray (-infinity, endpoint).

    The maximum endpoint itself is outside every listed strict lower ray; we
    output one unit beyond it to make the separation visually clear.  Running
    time is O(n) and auxiliary space is O(n) in the reporting certificate.
    """

    frozen = tuple(endpoints)
    if not frozen:
        raise ValueError("at least one endpoint is required")
    certificate = CoverEscapeCertificate(frozen, max(frozen) + 1)
    assert certificate.verify()
    return certificate


def format_fraction(value: Fraction) -> str:
    """Render a rational number without floating-point approximation."""

    return str(value.numerator) if value.denominator == 1 else str(value)


def run_demonstrations() -> None:
    """Run three exact, reproducible demonstrations and print certificates."""

    print("DEMO 1 — Finite diagonal lower bounds")
    families = [
        [Fraction(1, n) for n in range(1, 9)],
        [Fraction(1, 2 ** n) for n in range(1, 11)],
        [Fraction(7, 3), Fraction(2, 101), Fraction(11, 17), Fraction(1, 10_000)],
    ]
    for family in families:
        result = finite_diagonal_bound(family)
        print(
            f"  below {len(result.inputs):2d} values: "
            f"d = {format_fraction(result.bound)}, verified = {result.verify()}"
        )

    print("\nDEMO 2 — A lower ray defeats finite neighborhood proposals")
    radii = [Fraction(1, n * n) for n in range(1, 9)]
    neighborhood = stress_test_neighborhoods(radii)
    print(f"  proposed symmetric neighborhoods: {len(neighborhood.radii)}")
    print(f"  cutoff d = {format_fraction(neighborhood.cutoff)}")
    print(
        "  each neighborhood contains a selected point above d: "
        f"{neighborhood.verify()}"
    )

    print("\nDEMO 3 — Escape from finitely many lower rays")
    endpoint_sets = [
        [Fraction(-2), Fraction(0), Fraction(5, 2)],
        [Fraction(n) for n in range(12)],
        [Fraction(10 ** n) for n in range(6)],
    ]
    for endpoints in endpoint_sets:
        escape = escape_finite_lower_rays(endpoints)
        print(
            f"  {len(endpoints):2d} endpoints, escape point = "
            f"{format_fraction(escape.escape_point)}, verified = {escape.verify()}"
        )

    print(
        "\nInterpretation: these exact rational calculations model finite proof "
        "patterns. They do not numerically construct the full surreal number line."
    )


if __name__ == "__main__":
    run_demonstrations()

# Surreal Topology: Open Sets at Infinity

## A line too large for sequences

The ordinary real line is one of mathematics’ most familiar landscapes. Around every point, we can place successively smaller intervals: radius $1$, then $1/2$, then $1/3$, and so on. No matter how tiny a neighborhood we are later handed, one interval in that list fits inside it. This countable shrinking schedule is so natural that it is easy to mistake it for a universal feature of continuous space.

Conway’s surreal numbers show otherwise.

The surreal number line contains the real numbers, but it also contains infinitely large numbers greater than every integer and positive infinitesimals smaller than every positive real. More radically, it has room below *every countable list* of positive surreal numbers. Given positive surreals $u_0,u_1,u_2,\ldots$, there is another positive surreal $d$ satisfying

$$
0<d<u_n\qquad\text{for every }n\in\mathbb N.
$$

This single fact transforms the topology of the line. It means that no sequence can probe all scales near zero. However aggressively one chooses a countable list of positive sizes, the surreal line supplies a still smaller positive size beneath the entire list.

This article develops the consequences for the **order topology**: the topology generated by open intervals and open rays. The principal results are that the surreal line is Hausdorff, not first-countable, not metrizable, disconnected, and noncompact. Two questions suggested by the broader program—the extension of arbitrary real open sets and paracompactness—remain unresolved without additional structure, and we will state precisely what is missing.

## The interval topology

Let $\mathbf{No}$ denote a fixed universe-sized collection of surreal numbers, ordered in the usual way. Its order topology is generated by intervals

$$
(a,b)=\{x\in\mathbf{No}:a<x<b\}
$$

and the rays $(-\infty,b)$ and $(a,\infty)$. A set is open if each of its points lies in one of these basic intervals or rays contained in the set.

This topology is **Hausdorff**: if $x<y$, choose some $z$ with $x<z<y$; then $(-\infty,z)$ and $(z,\infty)$ separate $x$ from $y$. Thus distinct surreal numbers can be distinguished by disjoint neighborhoods, just as distinct real numbers can.

The resemblance soon ends.

A space is **first-countable at a point** if there is a countable family $B_0,B_1,B_2,\ldots$ of neighborhoods of that point such that every neighborhood contains at least one $B_n$. It is first-countable if this holds at every point. On the real line, the intervals $(-1/n,1/n)$ form such a family at zero. First countability is the mechanism that lets sequences describe closure, continuity, and convergence.

## The diagonal infinitesimal

The key theorem is a countable lower-bound principle.

**Countable Infinitesimal Theorem.** For every sequence $(u_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ of positive surreal numbers, there exists a positive surreal number $d$ such that $d<u_n$ for every $n$.

The construction uses Conway’s cut notation. Form the surreal number

$$
d=\{0\mid u_0,u_1,u_2,\ldots\}.
$$

The left options consist only of $0$, while every $u_n$ is a right option. Because $0<u_n$ for all $n$, this is a legitimate numerical cut. By the defining order properties of a surreal cut, $0<d$ and $d<u_n$ for every $n$.

For familiar real numbers the analogous statement is false. Take $u_n=1/(n+1)$. No positive real lies below all $u_n$. The surreal line fills that apparent gap with a new infinitesimal.

A small companion observation links this order-theoretic fact to topology.

**Positive-Point Lemma.** Every neighborhood of zero contains a positive surreal number.

Indeed, an order-topological neighborhood of zero contains a basic interval extending to the right of zero. Density of the surreal order—or, equivalently, a simple cut construction—provides a positive point in that interval.

These two statements power a diagonal argument against every proposed countable neighborhood basis.

## Why no countable microscope can work

Suppose, for contradiction, that $B_0,B_1,B_2,\ldots$ were a countable neighborhood basis at zero. From each $B_n$, choose a positive point $u_n\in B_n$. The Countable Infinitesimal Theorem supplies $d>0$ with $d<u_n$ for all $n$.

Now consider the open ray

$$
U=(-\infty,d).
$$

Since $0<d$, this is a neighborhood of zero. Yet no $B_n$ is contained in $U$, because $u_n$ belongs to $B_n$ while $u_n>d$. This contradicts the defining property of a neighborhood basis.

We have therefore proved the central result.

**Non-First-Countability Theorem.** The surreal line with its order topology is not first-countable.

The argument is more than a technical obstruction. It says that a countable sequence of “zoom levels” can never exhaust the local geometry. After every countable calibration, there remains an unregistered scale.

A standard consequence follows immediately.

**Non-Metrizability Theorem.** The surreal order topology is not induced by any metric.

Every metric space is first-countable: at a point $x$, the balls of radii $1,1/2,1/3,\ldots$ form a countable neighborhood basis. Since the surreal topology lacks such a basis at zero, no distance function can generate it. One may still compare surreal numbers algebraically, but no ordinary metric captures exactly which sets are open.

## A clopen frontier

The surreal line also splits naturally into two topological regions. Define the **finite-surreal region** by

$$
F=\{x\in\mathbf{No}: x<n\text{ for some }n\in\mathbb N\}.
$$

This terminology is one-sided: $F$ includes every negative surreal, however large in magnitude, because every negative number is below some natural number. What matters here is boundedness above by a natural number.

The set $F$ is open, since

$$
F=\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}(-\infty,n),
$$

and each ray in the union is open.

Less obvious is that $F$ is also closed. Suppose $x\notin F$. Then $x\ge n$ for every natural number $n$. The interval $(x-1,\infty)$ is a neighborhood of $x$. If some $y$ in that interval belonged to $F$, then $y<n$ for some $n$. Since $x<n+1$ would follow from $x<y+1<n+1$, we would contradict the fact that $x$ dominates every natural number. Hence $(x-1,\infty)$ lies in the complement of $F$, so the complement is open.

The region is nonempty because $0<1$, and it is proper because there exists a surreal number $M$ greater than every natural number. One may construct such an $M$ by a cut with all natural numbers on the left; taking a slightly larger surreal ensures strict inequalities.

Thus we obtain the following separation result.

**Clopen Finite-Region Theorem.** The set $F$ is nonempty, proper, open, and closed in the surreal order topology.

A topological space is **connected** if it cannot be divided into two disjoint nonempty open sets. A nonempty proper clopen set gives exactly such a division, namely $F$ and its complement. Therefore:

**Disconnectedness Theorem.** The surreal line with its order topology is disconnected.

This is a striking contrast with the real line. Although the surreal order has points between points, order density alone does not guarantee topological connectedness. The infinite scale creates a frontier that is invisible from either side: the finite side and the infinitely large side are both open.

## Why compactness fails

A space is **compact** if every open cover has a finite subcover. For linearly ordered spaces, compactness would in particular force the whole space to have extreme points under mild standard arguments. The surreal line has neither a greatest nor a least element: from any $x$, the numbers $x+1$ and $x-1$ lie strictly above and below it.

There is also a direct cover intuition. The family of rays

$$
\{(-\infty,a):a\in\mathbf{No}\}
$$

covers the entire surreal line, because every $x$ lies below $x+1$. Any finite selection has a largest endpoint $a$, and then a point greater than $a$ is uncovered. Hence:

**Noncompactness Theorem.** The surreal line with its order topology is not compact.

Noncompactness here is not merely ordinary unboundedness measured in real units. The surreal line continually creates new room beyond every finite collection of proposed bounds.

## What numerical experiments can—and cannot—show

Finite computation cannot instantiate the full surreal class or witness the failure of every countable basis. It can, however, display the diagonal logic on finite lists. Given positive rational numbers $u_0,\ldots,u_{N-1}$, the choice

$$
d=\frac12\min_{0\le n<N}u_n
$$

satisfies $0<d<u_n$ for all listed values. If each $u_n$ is selected from a candidate neighborhood $B_n$, then the ray $(-\infty,d)$ defeats all finitely many candidates at once. In the reals this procedure cannot survive an infinite list tending to zero; in the surreals, Conway’s cut construction does survive the entire countable list. The finite calculation is therefore an analogy for the selection-and-diagonal pattern, not a numerical proof of the surreal theorem.

Likewise, a finite sample can illustrate why finitely many initial rays never cover an unbounded ordered line: choose a point larger than their largest endpoint. The genuine theorem says that this escape remains possible in the full surreal order.

## The unfinished horizon

Two goals in the motivating program remain open in the present framework.

First, one would like every real open set to arise as the trace of a surreal-open set. A natural route begins with an ordered embedding $\iota:\mathbb R\to\mathbf{No}$. If this embedding is topological, then for a real open set $U$ one can consider the surreal union

$$
\bigcup_{(a,b)\subseteq U}(\iota(a),\iota(b)).
$$

Its inverse image should be $U$. Completing this argument requires a canonical embedding of all real numbers into the chosen surreal universe together with a proof that the embedding preserves the relevant topology. Those ingredients are not assumed here, so the extension theorem is a precise future target rather than an established result.

Second, the paracompactness question remains undecided. A space is **paracompact** if every open cover admits a locally finite open refinement. The clopen finite-region split hints that finer clopen partitions by infinitesimal scales may organize covers effectively. On the other hand, the enormous hierarchy of cofinality scales may obstruct local finiteness. Either direction requires new work.

Other natural goals include transferring non-first-countability from zero to every point via translations, proving stronger forms of disconnectedness such as total disconnectedness, and tracking how the results depend on the universe of surreal numbers under consideration.

## A new picture of continuity

The surreal line is orderly but not tame. It separates points cleanly, yet no metric describes its open sets. It has intervals and dense order, yet it falls apart into clopen regions. It supports local neighborhoods, yet no countable list can catalogue them. It stretches beyond every finite bound, and inside every countable descent it opens another infinitesimal level.

The governing idea is simple enough to fit in one cut:

$$
\{0\mid u_0,u_1,u_2,\ldots\}.
$$

From that cut comes a topology at infinity—and at the infinitesimal edge of zero—that behaves unlike the spaces built from ordinary measurement. The surreal numbers do not merely add exotic points to the real line. They change what it means to zoom in, to remain connected, and to cover a space.

# Surreal Topology: Countable Character, Clopen Cuts, and Open Sets at Infinity

**Aristotle**  
**19 July 2026**

## Abstract

We study the order topology on a fixed universe-sized surreal number line $\mathbf{No}$. The central order-theoretic input is a countable interpolation property: every sequence of positive surreal numbers admits a common positive strict lower bound. An explicit Conway cut gives this bound. We use it to prove that no countable family is cofinal in the neighborhood filter at zero, and consequently that the surreal order topology is not first-countable and not metrizable. We then define the lower finite region $F=\{x:x<n\text{ for some }n\in\mathbb N\}$ and prove that it is a nonempty proper clopen subset. Hence the surreal line is disconnected. Finally, the absence of a greatest element yields noncompactness, while the linear order guarantees the Hausdorff property. We distinguish these established conclusions from two unresolved objectives: extending arbitrary real open sets along a canonical real-to-surreal embedding, and deciding paracompactness. Numerical algorithms are included as finite models of the diagonal and open-cover arguments, with explicit discussion of the limits of finite simulation.

## 1. Introduction

The surreal numbers form an ordered field containing familiar number systems together with infinitesimal and infinitely large elements. Their construction by cuts is recursive: a surreal number is presented as $\{L\mid R\}$, where every member of the left set $L$ is strictly less than every member of the right set $R$. The resulting number lies above every element of $L$ and below every element of $R$.

Topologically, the most immediate structure on a linear order is its order topology. On $\mathbb R$, this topology is metrizable, connected, locally controlled by sequences, and noncompact. Some of those properties persist for $\mathbf{No}$, while others fail in characteristic ways. The surreal line remains Hausdorff and noncompact. It is, however, neither first-countable nor connected. The failure of first countability is driven not merely by the existence of individual infinitesimals but by a uniform countable interpolation principle: below every countable collection of positive scales there is a further positive scale.

This principle obstructs the basic metric habit of measuring neighborhoods by radii $1/n$. Given any countable collection of neighborhoods of zero, one may choose a positive point from each. A new positive surreal can then be inserted below all chosen points. The open ray ending at that new point is a neighborhood of zero containing none of the proposed basic neighborhoods. This is a diagonal argument internal to the order.

A second phenomenon occurs at infinity. The set of all surreals bounded above by some natural number is both open and closed. Its complement consists of surreals at least as large as every natural number. A unit interval below such a point remains in the complement. This clopen cut disconnects the line, despite the density of its order.

The paper is self-contained at the level of the order-topological arguments. Section 2 fixes the definitions. Section 3 proves the countable lower-bound theorem by a Conway cut. Section 4 derives non-first-countability and nonmetrizability. Section 5 constructs the clopen finite region and proves disconnectedness. Section 6 establishes noncompactness and records separation. Section 7 gives finite algorithms that illuminate the proofs without pretending to compute the full surreal universe. Section 8 discusses applications and interpretation. Section 9 isolates open questions, including real open-set extension and paracompactness.

## 2. Definitions and standing framework

### 2.1 Surreal cuts

We work with a fixed universe-sized surreal line $\mathbf{No}$. A cut

$$
\{L\mid R\}
$$

is numerical when every $\ell\in L$ satisfies $\ell<r$ for every $r\in R$. Its value lies strictly between all left and right options:

$$
\ell<\{L\mid R\}<r
$$

for every $\ell\in L$ and $r\in R$. Only this basic cut property is required below.

The order is unbounded in both directions. For every $x\in\mathbf{No}$,

$$
x-1<x<x+1.
$$

It is also densely ordered: whenever $x<y$, a surreal lies strictly between them; for example, the cut $\{x\mid y\}$ does so.

The phrase “fixed universe-sized” matters because the unrestricted collection of all surreal numbers is too large to be a set in the usual foundations. All families considered here, including countable families, are small relative to the chosen universe.

### 2.2 The order topology

The **order topology** on $\mathbf{No}$ is generated by open intervals

$$
(a,b)=\{x:a<x<b\},
$$

lower rays

$$
(-\infty,b)=\{x:x<b\},
$$

and upper rays

$$
(a,\infty)=\{x:a<x\}.
$$

A **neighborhood** of $x$ is a set containing an open set that contains $x$. A family $\mathcal B_x$ of neighborhoods of $x$ is a **neighborhood basis** if every neighborhood $U$ of $x$ contains some $B\in\mathcal B_x$.

A topological space is **first-countable at $x$** if $x$ has a countable neighborhood basis, and **first-countable** if this is true at every point. A topology is **metrizable** if it is generated by a metric. Every metrizable space is first-countable, because the balls

$$
B(x,1),B(x,1/2),B(x,1/3),\ldots
$$

form a neighborhood basis at $x$.

A subset is **clopen** if it is both closed and open. A space is **connected** if its only clopen subsets are the empty set and the whole space. A space is **compact** if every open cover admits a finite subcover. It is **Hausdorff** if every pair of distinct points has disjoint neighborhoods. Finally, a space is **paracompact** if every open cover has a locally finite open refinement, meaning that every point has a neighborhood meeting only finitely many sets in the refinement.

### 2.3 The lower finite region

Define

$$
F=\{x\in\mathbf{No}:\exists n\in\mathbb N,\ x<n\}.
$$

We call $F$ the **lower finite region**. This name should not be confused with the symmetric notion of finite magnitude. The set contains all negative surreals, including negative infinitely large ones, because each is less than a natural number. The exact one-sided definition is essential to the proof.

## 3. Countable interpolation below positive scales

The primary structural result is the following.

**Theorem 3.1 (Countable positive lower bound).** Let $(u_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ be a sequence of positive surreal numbers. Then there exists $d\in\mathbf{No}$ such that

$$
0<d<u_n
$$

for every $n\in\mathbb N$.

**Proof sketch.** Form the Conway cut

$$

$$

A **neighborhood** of $x$ is a set containing an open set that contains $x$. A family $\mathcal B_x$ of neighborhoods of $x$ is a **neighborhood basis** if every neighborhood $U$ of $x$ contains some $B\in\mathcal B_x$.

A topological space is **first-countable at $x$** if $x$ has a countable neighborhood basis, and **first-countable** if this is true at every point. A topology is **metrizable** if it is generated by a metric. Every metrizable space is first-countable, because the balls

$$
B(x,1),B(x,1/2),B(x,1/3),\ldots
$$

form a neighborhood basis at $x$.

A subset is **clopen** if it is both closed and open. A space is **connected** if its only clopen subsets are the empty set and the whole space. A space is **compact** if every open cover admits a finite subcover. It is **Hausdorff** if every pair of distinct points has disjoint neighborhoods. Finally, a space is **paracompact** if every open cover has a locally finite open refinement, meaning that every point has a neighborhood meeting only finitely many sets in the refinement.

### 2.3 The lower finite region

Define

$$
F=\{x\in\mathbf{No}:\exists n\in\mathbb N,\ x<n\}.
$$

We call $F$ the **lower finite region**. This name should not be confused with the symmetric notion of finite magnitude. The set contains all negative surreals, including negative infinitely large ones, because each is less than a natural number. The exact one-sided definition is essential to the proof.

## 3. Countable interpolation below positive scales

The primary structural result is the following.

**Theorem 3.1 (Countable positive lower bound).** Let $(u_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ be a sequence of positive surreal numbers. Then there exists $d\in\mathbf{No}$ such that

$$
0<d<u_n
$$

for every $n\in\mathbb N$.

**Proof sketch.** Form the Conway cut

$$
d=\{0\mid u_n:n\in\mathbb N\}.
$$

The cut is numerical because the hypothesis gives $0<u_n$ for every right option $u_n$. The defining inequalities for a numerical cut imply that its sole left option is below it and that it is below each right option. Therefore $0<d$ and $d<u_n$ for all $n$. $\square$

The theorem differs sharply from the Archimedean behavior of $\mathbb R$. For the positive real sequence $u_n=1/(n+1)$, no positive real $d$ satisfies $d<u_n$ for all $n$. In $\mathbf{No}$, the displayed cut creates precisely such a $d$.

The topological argument also requires positive points inside neighborhoods.

**Lemma 3.2 (Positive point in a zero-neighborhood).** If $U$ is a neighborhood of $0$ in the order topology, then there exists $x\in U$ with $x>0$.

**Proof sketch.** Since $U$ is a neighborhood, it contains a basic open interval around zero, or at least a half-interval extending from zero to some $y>0$. Choose $x$ strictly between $0$ and $y$. Such an $x$ exists by density; alternatively apply Theorem 3.1 to the constant sequence $u_n=y$ and obtain $0<x<y$. Then $x\in U$. $\square$

There is a useful conceptual distinction between Theorem 3.1 and ordinary density. Density inserts a point between one ordered pair. Theorem 3.1 simultaneously inserts a point below an entire countable positive family. It is this simultaneous interpolation that defeats countable local bases.

## 4. Countable character and metrizability

We now formalize the diagonal neighborhood argument.

**Theorem 4.1 (No countable neighborhood basis at zero).** There is no sequence of neighborhoods $(B_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ of zero such that every neighborhood of zero contains some $B_n$.

**Proof sketch.** Assume such a sequence exists. By Lemma 3.2, choose for each $n$ a positive surreal $u_n\in B_n$. Apply Theorem 3.1 to obtain $d>0$ satisfying $d<u_n$ for every $n$. The lower ray

$$
U=(-\infty,d)
$$

is an open neighborhood of zero. The basis property would give an index $n$ such that $B_n\subseteq U$. But $u_n\in B_n$ and $u_n>d$, so $u_n\notin U$. This contradiction proves the assertion. $\square$

**Theorem 4.2 (Failure of first countability).** The surreal order topology is not first-countable.

**Proof sketch.** First countability would in particular provide a countable neighborhood basis at zero, contradicting Theorem 4.1. $\square$

The proof shows that the **character** of zero—the least cardinality of a neighborhood basis—is uncountable. It does not, by itself, calculate the exact character.

**Corollary 4.3 (Nonmetrizability).** No metric induces the surreal order topology.

**Proof sketch.** Every metric topology is first-countable: balls of radii $1/(n+1)$ give a countable local basis at each point. Theorem 4.2 excludes this possibility. $\square$

This obstruction is topological rather than algebraic. One can define various distance-like quantities involving surreal arithmetic, but none can be an ordinary real-valued metric whose open balls generate exactly the order topology considered here.

A natural strengthening would assert failure of first countability at every point. Translation suggests the proof: if addition by $a$ is a homeomorphism, it carries a local basis at zero to one at $a$. Establishing the required continuity uniformly in the selected order-topological framework is left as future work, so our theorem is stated globally through failure at zero and does not claim the pointwise strengthening.

## 5. A nontrivial clopen cut

We next analyze the lower finite region $F$.

**Lemma 5.1 (Existence of an infinitely large surreal).** There exists $M\in\mathbf{No}$ such that

$$
n<M
$$

for every $n\in\mathbb N$.

**Proof sketch.** One may form a surreal with all natural numbers as left options and no right options,

$$
\omega=\{0,1,2,\ldots\mid\varnothing\}.
$$

By the cut inequalities, every natural number is less than $\omega$. Equivalently, a general small-family boundedness principle first supplies a common upper bound, and adding $1$ makes every comparison strict. $\square$

**Lemma 5.2 (Openness of the lower finite region).** The set $F$ is open.

**Proof sketch.** By definition,

$$
F=\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}(-\infty,n).
$$

Every lower ray is open in the order topology, and arbitrary unions of open sets are open. $\square$

**Lemma 5.3 (Closedness of the lower finite region).** The set $F$ is closed.

**Proof sketch.** It suffices to prove that its complement is open. Let $x\notin F$. Then

$$
x\ge n
$$

for every $n\in\mathbb N$. Consider the neighborhood $(x-1,\infty)$ of $x$. Suppose $y>x-1$ belonged to $F$. Then $y<n$ for some natural $n$. Adding $1$ gives

$$
x<y+1<n+1,
$$

so $x<n+1$, contradicting $x\notin F$. Therefore $(x-1,\infty)$ is contained in the complement of $F$, and that complement is open. $\square$

**Theorem 5.4 (Nontrivial clopen finite region).** The set $F$ is open and closed, is nonempty, and is not all of $\mathbf{No}$.

**Proof sketch.** Openness and closedness are Lemmas 5.2 and 5.3. It is nonempty because $0<1$, hence $0\in F$. It is proper because the surreal $M$ from Lemma 5.1 is greater than every natural number and therefore does not lie in $F$. $\square$

**Corollary 5.5 (Disconnectedness).** The surreal line with its order topology is disconnected.

**Proof sketch.** A connected space has no nonempty proper clopen subset. Theorem 5.4 supplies one. Equivalently, $F$ and $\mathbf{No}\setminus F$ are disjoint nonempty open sets whose union is the entire space. $\square$

This result may initially seem surprising because densely ordered sets often evoke intervals without gaps. The distinction is that connectedness of a linearly ordered topology requires a suitable order-completeness property as well as density. The cut between elements bounded above by a natural and elements dominating all naturals yields a topological separation even though there is no adjacent pair of points at its boundary.

## 6. Separation and compactness

**Theorem 6.1 (Hausdorff property).** The surreal order topology is Hausdorff.

**Proof sketch.** Let $x\ne y$, and assume without loss of generality that $x<y$. By order density, choose $a,b$ with

$$
x<a<b<y.
$$

Then $(-\infty,a)$ and $(b,\infty)$ are disjoint open neighborhoods of $x$ and $y$, respectively. Thus distinct points admit disjoint neighborhoods. $\square$

More directly, standard order-topological separation gives the same conclusion for every linear order.

**Theorem 6.2 (Noncompactness).** The surreal order topology is not compact.

**First proof sketch.** Consider the open cover

$$
\mathcal U=\{(-\infty,a):a\in\mathbf{No}\}.
$$

It covers $\mathbf{No}$ because $x\in(-\infty,x+1)$ for every $x$. Given finitely many selected rays with endpoints $a_1,\ldots,a_k$, let $a$ be their maximum. Their union is $(-\infty,a)$, which omits $a$ and every point above it. Hence no finite subfamily covers the line. $\square$

**Second proof sketch.** A nonempty compact subset of a linearly ordered Hausdorff space has a greatest element. If the whole surreal line were compact, it would have a greatest point $m$. But $m+1>m$, a contradiction. $\square$

The first proof is constructive at the level of covers and makes clear that noncompactness follows from unboundedness above. The same argument could use upper rays and unboundedness below.

## 7. Algorithms and finite numerical models

The theorems concern a universe-sized ordered field and cannot be exhaustively simulated. Nevertheless, finite rational computations can expose the logical architecture of the arguments.

### 7.1 Finite diagonal lower-bound algorithm

Given a nonempty finite list of positive rational numbers $u_0,\ldots,u_{N-1}$, define

$$
d=\frac12\min_{0\le i<N}u_i.
$$

Then $d>0$ and $d<u_i$ for every $i$. Finding the minimum takes $O(N)$ comparisons and $O(1)$ auxiliary space beyond the input. This is a finite analogue of Theorem 3.1.

The analogy has a strict boundary. For an infinite real sequence such as $u_n=1/(n+1)$, the infimum is zero, so no positive real diagonal bound exists. The surreal theorem replaces the finite minimum operation with the cut $\{0\mid u_0,u_1,\ldots\}$, which remains positive below the entire countable list.

### 7.2 Neighborhood-basis stress test

Represent a finite family of symmetric rational neighborhoods by radii $r_i>0$, with $B_i=(-r_i,r_i)$. Select the witness point $u_i=r_i/2\in B_i$. Compute

$$
d=\frac12\min_i u_i.
$$

The neighborhood $U=(-\infty,d)$ contains zero, while every $B_i$ contains $u_i>d$ and therefore is not a subset of $U$. The procedure takes $O(N)$ time. It exactly reproduces the selection and diagonal contradiction for a finite proposal.

It does not prove that a countable real basis fails—the real line has one. What changes for surreals is that the positive $d$ exists after countably many witnesses, not only finitely many.

### 7.3 Finite open-cover escape algorithm

For finitely many lower rays $(-\infty,a_i)$, calculate $m=\max_i a_i$ and output $m+1$. This point lies in none of the rays. The algorithm takes $O(N)$ time. It is the computational kernel of the noncompactness proof: every finite subfamily of the global ray cover leaves a point uncovered.

### 7.4 Demonstration protocol

A reproducible demonstration can evaluate several lists: ordinary positive fractions, rapidly decreasing fractions, and heterogeneous decimal scales. For each, it prints a diagonal lower bound and verifies all strict inequalities. It can also generate finite endpoint lists and print an escaping point. Assertions should be checked using exact rational arithmetic rather than floating-point approximations, ensuring that the displayed finite claims are exact.

## 8. Interpretation and applications

First countability is often invisible in elementary analysis because Euclidean spaces possess it automatically. It supports familiar equivalences: a point lies in the closure of a set precisely when a sequence from that set converges to it, and continuity can be tested by sequences. In spaces without first countability, sequences may not detect all local behavior; more general directed systems, called nets, are required. The surreal order topology therefore supplies a natural setting in which sequential intuition is insufficient.

Nonmetrizability has a similar message. A metric packages local structure into real-valued radii. The countable sequence of radii $1/(n+1)$ is always cofinal among positive real radii. Surreal neighborhoods carry more scales than any countable real calibration can register. Thus the obstruction is not a failure to invent a clever distance formula; it follows from an invariant of the topology itself.

The clopen finite region reflects a division between ordinary bounded-above behavior and infinite magnitude. Clopen sets are stable interfaces: each side can be studied without approaching the other through the topology. In dynamical language, a continuous image of a connected parameter interval cannot cross from one side to the other. We have proved disconnectedness, not the stronger assertion that every path is constant; total disconnectedness and total separatedness remain prospective refinements.

The Hausdorff property ensures that limits, when appropriately defined, are unique. Hence the topology is not pathological in the sense of failing point separation. Rather, it combines strong separation with excessive local character. This combination is useful when distinguishing independent topological properties: Hausdorff does not imply first-countable, metrizable, connected, or compact.

The results also clarify the phrase “open sets at infinity.” The complement of $F$ is open: every surreal dominating all natural numbers has a whole neighborhood consisting of surreals with the same domination property. Infinity is not merely approached as a missing endpoint. Infinitely large points occupy an open region separated from the lower finite region.

## 9. Real traces, paracompactness, and further questions

### 9.1 Extension of real open sets

Suppose an ordered embedding

$$
\iota:\mathbb R\longrightarrow\mathbf{No}
$$

has been fixed and proved to be a topological embedding. For an open set $U\subseteq\mathbb R$, a natural surreal-open candidate is

$$
\widetilde U=
\bigcup_{\substack{a,b\in\mathbb R\\(a,b)\subseteq U}}
(\iota(a),\iota(b)).
$$

Every interval in the union is surreal-open. If $\iota$ preserves and reflects the order topology, then $\iota^{-1}(\widetilde U)=U$: membership from left to right follows from $(a,b)\subseteq U$, while for $x\in U$, real openness supplies $a<x<b$ with $(a,b)\subseteq U$.

This conditional argument identifies the required mechanism, but the present framework does not assume a canonical embedding of all reals into the selected surreal universe together with its topological embedding theorem. Therefore the unconditional statement “every real open set has a surreal extension” is not claimed here. Constructing the embedding and proving its topological properties is a concrete next step.

### 9.2 Paracompactness

The established results do not decide whether the surreal order topology is paracompact. Nonmetrizability does not settle the question, because many paracompact spaces are nonmetrizable. Likewise, disconnectedness may either help by supplying clopen refinements or conceal large-cover obstructions.

A positive strategy would construct clopen partitions indexed by finite and infinitesimal scales and show that they refine arbitrary open covers locally finitely. A negative strategy would seek an open cover indexed by a hierarchy of cofinality levels for which every refinement fails local finiteness near some point. Either approach must respect the fixed universe and the smallness of indexing families.

### 9.3 Additional directions

Translation invariance should transfer the failure of countable character from zero to every point once continuity of addition and subtraction is established for this topology. Finer clopen cuts may lead to total separatedness, total disconnectedness, and the constancy of every path. Finally, the countable lower-bound theorem should be examined uniformly across universes, with explicit accounting of which families are small enough to form the required cuts.

## 10. Conclusion

The order topology on the surreal line exhibits a coherent set of properties:

1. every countable positive family has a common positive strict lower bound;
2. no countable neighborhood basis exists at zero;
3. the topology is not first-countable and therefore not metrizable;
4. the lower finite region is a nonempty proper clopen set, so the space is disconnected;
5. the space is not compact;
6. the space is Hausdorff.

All of these conclusions arise from elementary interactions between Conway cuts, order intervals, and standard topological definitions. The countable cut $\{0\mid u_0,u_1,\ldots\}$ defeats sequential local measurement, while the cut between natural-bounded and infinitely large surreals defeats connectedness. The resulting space is well separated but cannot be metrized, densely ordered but disconnected, and rich in points beyond every finite scale. \section{Introduction}

The surreal numbers form an ordered field containing familiar number systems together with infinitesimal and infinitely large elements. Their construction by cuts is recursive: a surreal number is presented as $\{L\mid R\}$, where every member of the left set $L$ is strictly less than every member of the right set $R$. The resulting number lies above every element of $L$ and below every element of $R$.

Topologically, the most immediate structure on a linear order is its order topology. On $\R$, this topology is metrizable, connected, locally controlled by sequences, and noncompact. Some of those properties persist for $\No$, while others fail in characteristic ways. The surreal line remains Hausdorff and noncompact. It is, however, neither first-countable nor connected. The failure of first countability is driven not merely by individual infinitesimals but by a uniform countable interpolation principle: below every countable collection of positive scales there is a further positive scale.

This principle obstructs the metric habit of measuring neighborhoods by radii $1/n$. Given any countable collection of neighborhoods of zero, one may choose a positive point from each. A new positive surreal can then be inserted below all chosen points. The open ray ending at that new point contains none of the proposed basic neighborhoods. This is a diagonal argument internal to the order.

A second phenomenon occurs at infinity. The set of all surreals bounded above by some natural number is both open and closed. Its complement consists of surreals at least as large as every natural number. A unit interval below such a point remains in the complement. This clopen cut disconnects the line despite the density of its order.

\section{Definitions and standing framework}

\subsection{Surreal cuts}

We work with a fixed universe-sized surreal line $\No$. A cut $\{L\mid R\}$ is \emph{numerical} when every $\ell\in L$ satisfies $\ell<r$ for every $r\in R$. Its value lies strictly between all left and right options:
\[
\ell<\{L\mid R\}<r
\]
for every $\ell\in L$ and $r\in R$. Only this cut property is required below.

The order is unbounded in both directions. For every $x\in\No$,
\[
x-1<x<x+1.
\]
It is densely ordered: whenever $x<y$, a surreal lies strictly between them; the cut $\{x\mid y\}$ is one such element.

The qualifier ``fixed universe-sized'' matters because the unrestricted collection of surreal numbers is too large to be a set in the usual foundations. All families considered here, including countable families, are small relative to the chosen universe.

\subsection{The order topology}

\begin{definition}
The \emph{order topology} on $\No$ is generated by intervals
\[
(a,b)=\{x:a<x<b\},
\]
lower rays $(-\infty,b)=\{x:x<b\}$, and upper rays $(a,\infty)=\{x:a<x\}$.
\end{definition}

A neighborhood of $x$ is a set containing an open set that contains $x$. A family $\mathcal B_x$ is a neighborhood basis if every neighborhood $U$ of $x$ contains some $B\in\mathcal B_x$.

\begin{definition}
A space is \emph{first-countable at $x$} if $x$ has a countable neighborhood basis, and \emph{first-countable} if this holds at every point. It is \emph{metrizable} if its topology is generated by a metric.
\end{definition}

Every metrizable space is first-countable, since balls of radii $1,1/2,1/3,\ldots$ form a neighborhood basis at each point.

A subset is \emph{clopen} if it is closed and open. A space is connected if its only clopen subsets are the empty set and the entire space. It is compact if every open cover has a finite subcover, Hausdorff if distinct points have disjoint neighborhoods, and paracompact if every open cover has a locally finite open refinement.

\begin{definition}
The \emph{lower finite region} is
\[
F=\{x\in\No:\exists n\in\N,\ x<n\}.
\]
\end{definition}

This is a one-sided notion. It contains every negative surreal, including negative infinitely large ones, since each is below a natural number. That exact definition is essential below.

\section{Countable interpolation below positive scales}

\begin{theorem}[Countable positive lower bound]
Let $(u_n)_{n\in\N}$ be a sequence of positive surreal numbers. Then there exists $d\in\No$ such that
\[
0<d<u_n
\]
for every $n\in\N$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Form the Conway cut
\[
d=\{0\mid u_n:n\in\N\}.
\]
The cut is numerical because $0<u_n$ for every right option. The defining inequalities for a numerical cut place its value above its sole left option and below each right option. Thus $0<d$ and $d<u_n$ for every $n$.
\end{proof}

The theorem differs sharply from Archimedean behavior. For the real sequence $u_n=1/(n+1)$, no positive real $d$ lies below every $u_n$. The surreal cut creates precisely such an element.

\begin{lemma}[Positive point in a zero-neighborhood]
If $U$ is a neighborhood of $0$ in the order topology, then some $x\in U$ satisfies $x>0$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
The set $U$ contains a basic open set around zero and hence contains a half-interval extending from zero to some $y>0$. Choose $x$ strictly between $0$ and $y$ by density. Alternatively, apply the preceding theorem to the constant sequence with value $y$. Then $0<x<y$, so $x\in U$.
\end{proof}

Density inserts a point between one ordered pair. The theorem simultaneously inserts a point below an entire countable positive family. This simultaneous interpolation defeats countable local bases.

\section{Countable character and metrizability}

\begin{theorem}[No countable neighborhood basis at zero]
There is no sequence of neighborhoods $(B_n)_{n\in\N}$ of zero such that every neighborhood of zero contains some $B_n$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Assume such a sequence exists. Choose, from each $B_n$, a positive surreal $u_n$. The countable positive lower-bound theorem gives $d>0$ with $d<u_n$ for all $n$. The lower ray
\[
U=(-\infty,d)
\]
is an open neighborhood of zero. The basis property would give $n$ with $B_n\subseteq U$. But $u_n\in B_n$ and $u_n>d$, so $u_n\notin U$, a contradiction.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Failure of first countability]
The surreal order topology is not first-countable.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
First countability would provide a countable neighborhood basis at zero, contrary to the preceding theorem.
\end{proof}

The proof shows that the character of zero, the least cardinality of a neighborhood basis there, is uncountable. It does not calculate the exact character.

\begin{corollary}[Nonmetrizability]
No metric induces the surreal order topology.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
Every metric topology is first-countable, using balls of radii $1/(n+1)$. The preceding theorem excludes this possibility.
\end{proof}

This obstruction is topological rather than algebraic. Distance-like expressions may be defined using surreal arithmetic, but no ordinary metric can generate exactly this topology.

Translation suggests a strengthening to failure of first countability at every point: a homeomorphism $x\mapsto x+a$ would transfer local bases between zero and $a$. Establishing the required continuity uniformly in the selected framework remains future work, so we do not claim that pointwise strengthening here.

\section{A nontrivial clopen cut}

\begin{lemma}[Existence of an infinitely large surreal]
There exists $M\in\No$ such that $n<M$ for every $n\in\N$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Form
\[
\omega=\{0,1,2,\ldots\mid\varnothing\}.
\]
Every natural number is a left option and is therefore strictly below $\omega$. One may equivalently obtain a common upper bound for the countable family and add $1$ to make all comparisons strict.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Openness of the lower finite region]
The set $F$ is open.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
By definition,
\[
F=\bigcup_{n\in\N}(-\infty,n).
\]
Each lower ray is open, and arbitrary unions of open sets are open.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Closedness of the lower finite region]
The set $F$ is closed.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Let $x\notin F$. Then $x\ge n$ for every $n\in\N$. Consider $(x-1,\infty)$. If $y>x-1$ belonged to $F$, then $y<n$ for some natural $n$. Adding $1$ would give
\[
x<y+1<n+1,
\]
contradicting $x\notin F$. Thus $(x-1,\infty)$ is contained in the complement of $F$. The complement is open, so $F$ is closed.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Nontrivial clopen finite region]
The set $F$ is open and closed, nonempty, and not equal to $\No$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Openness and closedness are the preceding lemmas. Since $0<1$, we have $0\in F$. The infinitely large surreal $M$ above is greater than every natural number and hence does not lie in $F$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Disconnectedness]
The surreal line with its order topology is disconnected.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
A connected space has no nonempty proper clopen subset, while $F$ is such a subset. Equivalently, $F$ and $\No\setminus F$ are disjoint nonempty open sets whose union is $\No$.
\end{proof}

The result illustrates that density alone does not ensure connectedness for an ordered topology. A suitable order-completeness property is also needed. The finite/infinite cut yields a separation even though there is no adjacent pair of points at its boundary.

\section{Separation and compactness}

\begin{theorem}[Hausdorff property]
The surreal order topology is Hausdorff.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Let $x<y$. By density choose $a,b$ with $x<a<b<y$. Then $(-\infty,a)$ and $(b,\infty)$ are disjoint open neighborhoods of $x$ and $y$, respectively.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Noncompactness]
The surreal order topology is not compact.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Consider the open cover
\[
\mathcal U=\{(-\infty,a):a\in\No\}.
\]
It covers $\No$, because $x\in(-\infty,x+1)$ for every $x$. Given finitely many chosen rays with endpoints $a_1,\ldots,a_k$, let $a$ be their maximum. Their union is $(-\infty,a)$, which omits $a$ and every larger point. No finite subfamily covers $\No$.
\end{proof}

Alternatively, a nonempty compact subset of a linearly ordered Hausdorff space has a greatest element. Compactness of the whole line would therefore produce a greatest surreal $m$, contradicted by $m+1>m$.

For finitely many lower rays $(-\infty,a_i)$, calculate $m=\max_i a_i$ and output $m+1$. This point lies in none of the rays. The algorithm takes $O(N)$ time and is the computational kernel of the noncompactness proof.

\section{Interpretation and applications}

First countability supports familiar sequential characterizations of closure and continuity. In spaces without it, sequences may not detect all local behavior; more general directed systems, or nets, are needed. The surreal order topology is therefore a natural setting in which sequential intuition is insufficient.

Nonmetrizability carries a related message. A metric packages local structure into real-valued radii, and the radii $1/(n+1)$ are countably cofinal among positive real radii. Surreal neighborhoods possess scales beyond any countable real calibration. The obstruction is thus invariant under every attempt to replace one metric formula by another.

The clopen lower finite region reflects a division between natural-bounded behavior and infinite magnitude. Each side is open, so infinitely large points do not merely serve as missing endpoints approached from finite values; they occupy a topologically separated region. In dynamical terms, a continuous image of a connected interval cannot cross from one side to the other. We have proved disconnectedness, not the stronger claim that every path is constant.

The Hausdorff property ensures uniqueness of limits when limits are appropriately defined. The topology is consequently not pathological through poor point separation. Rather, it combines strong separation with excessive local character, illustrating that Hausdorffness implies none of first countability, metrizability, connectedness, or compactness.

\section{Real traces, paracompactness, and further questions}

\subsection{Extension of real open sets}

Suppose an ordered embedding
\[
\iota:\R\longrightarrow\No
\]
has been fixed and shown to be a topological embedding. For an open $U\subseteq\R$, define the candidate
\[
\widetilde U=
\bigcup_{\substack{a,b\in\R\\(a,b)\subseteq U}}
(\iota(a),\iota(b)).
\]
Every interval in this union is surreal-open. If $\iota$ preserves and reflects the order topology, then $\iota^{-1}(\widetilde U)=U$. One inclusion follows from $(a,b)\subseteq U$; for the other, real openness supplies $a<x<b$ with $(a,b)\subseteq U$ whenever $x\in U$.

This conditional argument identifies the mechanism, but the present framework does not assume a canonical embedding of all reals into the chosen surreal universe together with its topological embedding theorem. Thus the unconditional extension statement is not claimed. Constructing that embedding and proving its topological properties is a concrete next step.

\subsection{Paracompactness}

The established results do not decide whether the surreal order topology is paracompact. Nonmetrizability does not settle the issue, since many paracompact spaces are nonmetrizable. Disconnectedness may help by supplying clopen refinements, or it may conceal large-cover obstructions.

A positive strategy would construct clopen partitions indexed by finite and infinitesimal scales and prove that they refine arbitrary open covers locally finitely. A negative strategy would seek an open cover indexed by a hierarchy of cofinality levels for which every refinement fails local finiteness near some point. Either approach must track the fixed universe and the smallness of indexing families.

\subsection{Additional directions}

Translation invariance should transfer failure of countable character from zero to every point once continuity of addition and subtraction has been established. Finer clopen cuts may yield total separatedness, total disconnectedness, and constancy of paths. Finally, the countable lower-bound theorem should be stated uniformly across universes, with explicit accounting of which families are small enough to form the required cuts.

\section{Conclusion}

The order topology on the surreal line has the following established properties. Every countable positive family admits a common positive strict lower bound. No countable neighborhood basis exists at zero, so the topology is not first-countable and not metrizable. The lower finite region is a nonempty proper clopen set, so the line is disconnected. The topology is noncompact and Hausdorff.

These conclusions arise from elementary interactions between Conway cuts, order intervals, and standard topological definitions. The countable cut $\{0\mid u_0,u_1,\ldots\}$ defeats sequential local measurement, while the division between natural-bounded and infinitely large surreals defeats connectedness. The resulting space is well separated but cannot be metrized, densely ordered but disconnected, and rich in points beyond every finite scale. Real open-set extension and paracompactness remain sharply formulated questions for subsequent work.

    endpoints: tuple[Fraction, ...]

    """Validate and freeze a nonempty family of positive rational values."""

    if any(value <= 0 for value in frozen):

    """Return half the minimum of a finite positive rational family.

"""Exact finite demonstrations inspired by the topology of surreal numbers.

The full surreal line is not a finite numerical object.  These examples use
Fractions to demonstrate three proof patterns exactly:
(1) diagonalizing below a finite positive family,
(2) defeating a finite proposal of neighborhoods of zero, and
(3) escaping every finite selection from an unbounded lower-ray cover.

from __future__ import annotations

from dataclasses import dataclass
from fractions import Fraction
from typing import Iterable, Sequence


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class DiagonalCertificate:
    """A positive number certified to lie below every listed positive value."""

    inputs: tuple[Fraction, ...]
    bound: Fraction

    def verify(self) -> bool:
        return self.bound > 0 and all(self.bound < value for value in self.inputs)


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class NeighborhoodCertificate:
    """Witnesses that no listed symmetric neighborhood fits in (-infinity, d)."""

    radii: tuple[Fraction, ...]
    selected_points: tuple[Fraction, ...]
    cutoff: Fraction

    def verify(self) -> bool:
        return (
            len(self.radii) == len(self.selected_points)
            and self.cutoff > 0
            and all(radius > 0 for radius in self.radii)
            and all(
                0 < point < radius and point > self.cutoff
                for radius, point in zip(self.radii, self.selected_points)
            )
        )


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class CoverEscapeCertificate:
    """A point lying beyond every endpoint of finitely many lower rays."""

    endpoints: tuple[Fraction, ...]
    escape_point: Fraction

    def verify(self) -> bool:
        return bool(self.endpoints) and all(
            self.escape_point >= endpoint for endpoint in self.endpoints
        )


def as_positive_tuple(values: Iterable[Fraction]) -> tuple[Fraction, ...]:
    """Validate and freeze a nonempty family of positive rational values."""

    frozen = tuple(values)
    if not frozen:
        raise ValueError("at least one value is required")
    if any(value <= 0 for value in frozen):
        raise ValueError("all values must be strictly positive")
    return frozen


def finite_diagonal_bound(values: Iterable[Fraction]) -> DiagonalCertificate:
    """Return half the minimum of a finite positive rational family.

    Time complexity is O(n); auxiliary space is O(n) because the iterable is
    frozen for certificate reporting (the minimum itself needs only O(1)).
    """

    frozen = as_positive_tuple(values)
    certificate = DiagonalCertificate(frozen, min(frozen) / 2)
    assert certificate.verify()
    return certificate

    radii: Iterable[Fraction],
) -> NeighborhoodCertificate:
    """Defeat finitely many symmetric neighborhoods (-r_i, r_i).

    Select u_i = r_i/2 in each neighborhood, then choose a positive cutoff d
    below every u_i.  Since u_i > d, no neighborhood is contained in the lower
    ray (-infinity, d).  The computation takes O(n) time.
    """

    frozen = as_positive_tuple(radii)
    selected = tuple(radius / 2 for radius in frozen)
    cutoff = min(selected) / 2
    certificate = NeighborhoodCertificate(frozen, selected, cutoff)
    assert certificate.verify()
    return certificate

    endpoints: Sequence[Fraction],
) -> CoverEscapeCertificate:
    """Find a point omitted by every lower ray (-infinity, endpoint).

    The maximum endpoint itself is outside every listed strict lower ray; we
    output one unit beyond it to make the separation visually clear.  Running
    time is O(n) and auxiliary space is O(n) in the reporting certificate.
    """

    frozen = tuple(endpoints)
    if not frozen:
        raise ValueError("at least one endpoint is required")
    certificate = CoverEscapeCertificate(frozen, max(frozen) + 1)
    assert certificate.verify()
    return certificate

    return str(value.numerator) if value.denominator == 1 else str(value)

        [Fraction(1, 2 ** n) for n in range(1, 11)],
        [Fraction(7, 3), Fraction(2, 101), Fraction(11, 17), Fraction(1, 10_000)],

            f"d = {format_fraction(result.bound)}, verified = {result.verify()}"

    radii = [Fraction(1, n * n) for n in range(1, 9)]
    neighborhood = stress_test_neighborhoods(radii)
    print(f"  proposed symmetric neighborhoods: {len(neighborhood.radii)}")

    print(
        "  each neighborhood contains a selected point above d: "
        f"{neighborhood.verify()}"
    )

    print("\nDEMO 3 — Escape from finitely many lower rays")
    endpoint_sets = [
        [Fraction(-2), Fraction(0), Fraction(5, 2)],
        [Fraction(n) for n in range(12)],
        [Fraction(10 ** n) for n in range(6)],
    ]
    for endpoints in endpoint_sets:

        print(
            f"  {len(endpoints):2d} endpoints, escape point = "
            f"{format_fraction(escape.escape_point)}, verified = {escape.verify()}"
        )

    print(
        "\nInterpretation: these exact rational calculations model finite proof "
        "patterns. They do not numerically construct the full surreal number line."
    )
